newsitem.title: CHINA: China-backed paper links war games-island dispute.
newsitem.headline: China-backed paper links war games-island dispute.

text.p: A Beijing-backed newspaper on Tuesday linked rare Chinese military exercises in the Gobi Desert to the dispute with Japan over a group of islands in the East China Sea, but analysts said the link was far fetched.

The Wen Wei Po newspaper, mouthpiece of the Communist Party in Hong Kong, gave prominent coverage to the air force exercises and the simmering row over the uninhabited islands -- claimed by Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei -- and ran the stories together in a box.
"Putting the two stories together gives readers the impression that China has the military ability to take the islands," said a Beijing-based Chinese analyst who asked not to be identified.
The Beijing office of the newspaper declined to comment.

But another analyst said the newspaper may have been trying to placate Chinese readers in Hong Kong who have become angry with Japan over the disputed islands, which are known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus.
Newspapers in Beijing also reported the exercises, which involved advanced military aircraft and the best of China's air force.
The war games broke the taboo of not using live ammunition in "confrontational drills," the Liberation Army Daily said.
Much air force training had begun shifting in nature from defensive-oriented to offensive-oriented, the newspapers said.

They were the first military exercises reported by China since it test-fired missiles and held live-fire war games in the Taiwan Strait in a show of force intended to intimidate Taiwan ahead of its first direct presidential elections last March.
Western analysts said they doubted that China was trying to use these exercises to intimidate Japan.
"The Chinese have been at great pains to lower the temperature on the dispute with Japan over the Diaoyu/Senkakus," a Western diplomat said by telephone.
"They've not...allowed sentiment to run too strongly here," the diplomat said. "I don't think they are in aggressive mode at the moment... They haven't been really inflammatory.
"It's intended as confidence building rather than an extra threat," the diplomat said of the newspaper reports that China had conducted exercises in its northwestern Gobi Desert.
Robert Karniol, Bangkok-based Asia/Pacific editor of Jane's Defence Weekly, agreed. "It seems an extreme stretch of the imagination to try to link that exercise to the Diaoyu islands," Karniol said.
A long-dormant dispute over the islands erupted in July after a rightist Japanese group erected a lighthouse and a war memorial on the islands to bolster Tokyo's sovereignty claim.

It intensified this month after Tokyo sent patrol ships to repel private Taiwan vesels that tried to approach the islands. The move touched off anti-Japanese protests in Chinese communities in Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Last week, China lodged a strong protest with Japan and called in its charge d'affaires in Beijing, warning of serious damage to bilateral ties if Tokyo failed to stop its rightists setting foot on the islands.
More than 100 Chinese nationalists urged China's top military brass to send warships to the islands to tear down the structures built by the group, the Japan Youth Federation.
A group of Hong Kong legislators urged China to send warships to guard the dispute islands, while Japan called for calm from the rival claimants.
